Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: Difficulty breathing after recent insect sting (bee/wasp not specified); localized rash at sting site on arm; reports slight right-sided lip swelling sensation and “tongue feels weird”; anxiety about potential worsening.
- Onset/duration/progression: Sting occurred a few minutes prior to consult; breathing discomfort not acute at time of call; local redness present; no significant swelling at site reported; no medications taken yet.
- Past medical history: Eczema. Occasional anxiety/panic episodes. No history of anaphylaxis. Never prescribed an epinephrine auto-injector.
- Medications: None reported currently; no antihistamines taken yet. Medication reconciliation not completed.
- Social history: Lives alone; employed as a computer scientist. Has a cat at home. No known pet or food allergies.
- Allergies: Penicillin.

Objective:
- General/respiratory (via video): Speaking in full sentences; breathing appears normal; no audible stridor or respiratory distress observed.
- Lips/oral cavity (via video): No visible lip swelling on inspection; oropharynx visualized with “ah”—no obvious soft tissue swelling observed.
- Skin (arm; side not specified): Localized mild erythema with puncture mark; blotchy rash; patient denies notable swelling; clinician could not appreciate swelling on video.
- Vitals: Not obtained (telehealth).
- Investigations: None performed.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Localized reaction to insect sting:
   - Assessment: Localized allergic reaction without current features of anaphylaxis.
   - Differential diagnosis (if symptoms progress): Early anaphylaxis; cellulitis (if spreading redness, warmth, pain).
   - Investigations planned: None now; consider blood testing if reactions become recurrent or if nonspecific rashes develop.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Start OTC chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet by mouth, up to six times daily as needed.
     - Alternative: OTC once-daily antihistamine (agent/dose/route not documented).
     - Monitor the sting site; if redness spreads, becomes hot/painful, or systemic signs develop, seek reassessment for possible antibiotic therapy.
     - Education provided on signs of anaphylaxis (lip/tongue swelling, difficulty breathing, stridor); information link provided.
   - Safety net: If any airway symptoms or rapid progression occur, go to the ER immediately or call emergency services; otherwise, contact clinic if symptoms worsen or do not improve.
   - Referrals: None at this time.

2. Anxiety related to acute event:
   - Assessment: Situational anxiety; no acute panic episode observed on call.
   - Treatment planned: Reassurance; advised low threshold to recontact clinic if concerns persist or escalate.
   - Referrals: None.

3. Drug allergy:
   - Assessment: Penicillin allergy (patient-reported).
   - Treatment planned: Avoid penicillin-class antibiotics; ensure allergy documented in chart.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: Full medication list and reconciliation; vitals; past surgical history; smoking/alcohol/substance use; detailed review of systems; vaccination status not discussed. Exact sting location (side) not documented.
- Internal conflicts: Patient stated age 27 but also reported DOB 11/17/1991 (conflict noted). Insect type uncertain (bee vs wasp; sting vs bite).
- Transcript quality: Minor gaps/inaudible filler words; overall history and exam findings understandable. Telehealth limitations acknowledged.
